strengths: Principled and unified perspective: The paper neatly organizes prior particle- and tree-based test-time diffusion methods into a coherent BFS/DFS framework and provides a clear ablation of the search design space (tempering, scoring functions, and resampling schemes).

Solid theoretical contribution: Proposition 1 and Theorem 1 provide a valuable theoretical connection showing that training-free guidance with recurrence asymptotically corresponds to annealed Langevin MCMC, providing formal justification for recurrent gradient guidance.

Adaptive compute allocation via DFS: The proposed DFS-style non-linear backtracking mechanism is intuitive and effectively demonstrates instance-dependent test-time compute allocation (spending more compute on harder prompts).

Broad and versatile experimental validation: The method is evaluated across diverse domains, including text-to-image synthesis (CompBench), robot trajectory planning (PointMaze), offline reinforcement learning (D4RL), policy distillation, and ImageNet class-conditional generation.
weaknesses: Unreliable FID evaluation in Section 5.4: In the ImageNet experiments, FID is computed using only 256 samples. Standard generative modeling benchmarks require 10k to 50k samples, as FID on a few hundred samples suffers from severe sample bias and variance.

Hyperparameter sensitivity and search burden: The proposed framework introduces multiple interacting hyperparameters (e.g., threshold schedules, backtracking depth, recurrence steps, step sizes, and temperatures). As detailed in Appendices E.3 and E.4, extensive per-task tuning was necessary, which poses practical challenges for general test-time deployment.

Minor presentation issues and typos: There are unfinished sentences and typos in the draft, such as an incomplete sentence on page 1 ('Project page at .'), typos in Figure 4 headers ('Parero Curves'), and missing punctuation/captions in Section 5.2/Figure 6.

strengths: Unifying Conceptual Framework: The paper provides a clean, principled formulation that bridges classical search algorithms (BFS, DFS) with gradient-based local search (annealed Langevin MCMC) for inference-time scaling in diffusion models.

Theoretical Foundation: Proposition 1 and Theorem 1 formally connect training-free guidance with recurrence to annealed Langevin MCMC in the continuous limit, accompanied by a Wasserstein-2 convergence bound. This offers valuable theoretical justification for why recurrent guidance mitigates out-of-distribution drift.

Adaptive Compute Allocation via DFS: The proposed DFS-style non-linear search with adaptive backtracking dynamically scales compute based on instance difficulty and verifier feedback, outperforming fixed-schedule particle filtering baselines with lower computational overhead.

Comprehensive and Diverse Evaluation: The framework is rigorously evaluated across distinct domains, including text-to-image synthesis (SDXL, SSD-1B on CompBench), long-horizon trajectory planning (PointMaze), and offline RL (D4RL benchmark), demonstrating wide applicability.

Pragmatic Solutions to Practical Pitfalls: The double-verifier strategy for mitigating reward hacking and over-optimization in gradient-based guidance is intuitive and empirically effective, drawing a neat parallel to Double Q-learning.
weaknesses: Hyperparameter Complexity: The framework introduces multiple sensitive hyperparameters (e.g., backtrack depth $\Delta T$, threshold schedule $\delta_t$, tempering parameter $\gamma$, recurrence steps $N_{\text{recur}}$, step sizes $\bar{\rho}$ and $\bar{\mu}$). As demonstrated in Appendix Table 9, these settings vary noticeably across environments, posing a non-trivial tuning overhead in practical deployment.

Small Sample Size for FID Calculation: In Section 5.4 and Appendix E.5, FID on conditional ImageNet generation is reported using only 256 samples. Standard Fréchet Inception Distance calculations typically require thousands (e.g., 10k–50k) of samples, as estimates with very small sample sizes suffer from substantial bias and high variance.

Disconnection Between RL Experiments and Advanced Tree Search: In Section 5.3.2 (Offline RL), the global search component simplifies to Best-of-N because particle budgets are kept small ($N=2$ to $4$), meaning the advantages of adaptive DFS or unified BFS are not demonstrated on this benchmark.

Minor Presentation Polish: A few placeholder texts and typographical errors remain, such as an incomplete sentence at the end of the abstract ('Project page at .'), 'inheritability biased' (page 3), and 'successfual' (Figure 5 caption).

strengths: Timely and relevant topic: Inference-time compute scaling for diffusion models is an important and active area of research, paralleling recent developments in test-time scaling for language models.

Unifying perspective on tree and particle search: The paper systematically categorizes the design space of linear particle/tree methods (tempering, scoring functions, and resampling strategies), helping clarify the relationship between recent approaches such as FK-steering, DAS, and SVDD.
Adaptive compute via DFS: The DFS-style search with backtracking provides a clean conceptual framework for allocating compute adaptively based on instance difficulty.

Theoretical connection: Proposition 1 and Theorem 1 provide a nice formal perspective connecting recurrent training-free guidance to annealed Langevin MCMC in the continuous limit, supported by a convergence bound in Wasserstein distance.

Breadth of evaluation domains: The method is tested across a diverse range of tasks, including text-to-image generation (CompBench, ImageNet), long-horizon trajectory planning (PointMaze), and offline RL policy distillation.
weaknesses: Limited novelty in search components: The improved BFS is largely a combination of existing building blocks—specifically, the increasing tempering schedule and SSP resampling from DAS (Kim et al., 2025) combined with the Max scoring function from FK-steering (Singhal et al., 2025a). The algorithmic novelty of the unified BFS is therefore somewhat incremental.

Global search (BFS/DFS) omitted in offline RL: A central claim of the paper is the joint scaling of global search and local search. However, in the offline RL experiments (Section 5.3.2 and Section E.4), the authors explicitly state that neither BFS nor DFS was used due to the small particle budget; instead, only naive Best-of-N was used alongside local search. This undermines the narrative of unified search on one of the main benchmark domains.

Flawed evaluation setup on ImageNet: In Section 5.4 and Table 5, FID is computed on only 256 generated samples. Fréchet Inception Distance is heavily sample-size dependent and notoriously unstable/biased at such small sample counts (standard protocol requires at least 10k–50k samples). Reporting FID-256 with values in the 118–171 range makes the metric virtually uninterpretable.

Sensitivity and tuning of the DFS threshold: The efficiency and behavior of DFS fundamentally rely on the threshold schedule $\delta_t$. Setting this threshold requires prior knowledge of the verifier's numerical range or an extensive sweep (as shown in Figure 7), which reduces the practical 'plug-and-play' applicability of adaptive test-time search.

Signs of rushed presentation and typos: There is an incomplete placeholder in the Abstract ('Project page at .'), prominent typos in Figure 4 ('Parero Curves with Different Local Search Steps' and 'Parero Curves with BFS and DFS'), Figure 5 caption ('successfual sample'), and Section E.5 ('double-verfier').

strengths: Principled and unified perspective: The paper successfully bridges classical search principles (local hill-climbing and global tree search like BFS/DFS) with test-time scaling in diffusion models, offering a coherent conceptual framework.

Theoretical connection: Proposition 1 nicely establishes the equivalence between recurrent training-free guidance and annealed Langevin MCMC in the continuous limit, clarifying why recurrence prevents trajectory drift and adversarial/out-of-distribution modes.

Diverse cross-domain empirical evaluation: The proposed search mechanisms are validated across three distinct problem domains: long-horizon maze planning (PointMaze Giant/Ultra), offline reinforcement learning (D4RL locomotion), and image generation (CompBench and conditional ImageNet).

Dynamic compute allocation via DFS: The DFS formulation naturally performs difficulty-aware inference scaling—adaptively backtracking more on difficult instances and less on easy ones without requiring pre-labeled instance difficulty.
weaknesses: Narrow evaluation scope in certain experiments: For ImageNet conditional generation, experiments are only conducted on two specific classes (labels 222 and 444) with 256 samples each, which is notably limited compared to standard 50,000-sample / multi-class evaluation protocols.

Underutilization of global search in offline RL: On the D4RL benchmark (Table 1), the method uses only simple Best-of-N with 2 or 4 particles rather than BFS or DFS, making this section essentially an evaluation of recurrent local guidance rather than the broader tree-search framework.

High hyperparameter tuning overhead: As evidenced in Section C.5, Table 3, and the limitations section, the framework introduces multiple sensitive parameters (temperature $\tau_t$, evaluation timesteps $S$, backtracking depth $\Delta T$, threshold schedule $\delta_t$, and guidance gains $\bar{\rho}, \bar{\mu}$) which vary across tasks and currently require extensive grid search.

Wall-clock and memory overhead: While sample efficiency is plotted against function evaluations (NFEs), the paper does not thoroughly discuss the practical runtime and memory implications of storing intermediate paths and executing backtracking/resampling branches in batched GPU environments.

strengths: Timely and important problem: adapts principles of classical search (local hill-climbing / Langevin MCMC, global BFS and DFS) to scale test-time compute in diffusion models, mirroring recent progress in test-time scaling for LLMs.
Principled theoretical connection: Proposition 1 provides a neat formal unification showing that recurrent training-free guidance in the continuous limit converges to annealed Langevin MCMC.

Diverse evaluation domains: unlike many concurrent works that focus solely on text-to-image generation, this work evaluates across trajectory planning (PointMaze Giant and Ultra), offline reinforcement learning (D4RL), and vision benchmarks (CompBench, ImageNet).

Clear efficiency gains over naive best-of-N sampling: empirical scaling curves demonstrate that intermediate verification, BFS-resampling/pruning, and DFS backtracking achieve better score/accuracy frontiers per function evaluation.
weaknesses: Limited scale of ImageNet evaluation: the conditional ImageNet experiment in Section 5.3.2 is only conducted on two specific classes (label 222 and 444) with 256 samples each. Evaluating across a representative cross-section or standard benchmark suite would be significantly more convincing.

Decoupling in Offline RL experiments: for the D4RL locomotion tasks (Section 5.2 and Appendix E.2), the method does not actually utilize the proposed BFS or DFS global search algorithms due to small particle budgets (2-4 particles), relying instead on standard Best-of-N. This diminishes the empirical demonstration of the global tree search algorithms on RL tasks.

High hyperparameter tuning overhead: as acknowledged in Section 6, the framework introduces multiple sensitive parameters per task (eval step set $S$, temperature schedules $\tau_t$, backtracking depth $\Delta T$, threshold schedules $\delta_t$, recurrence steps $N_{recur}$), which require non-trivial task-specific grid searching (as detailed in Appendix E).

Conceptual overlap with concurrent work: tree search and Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) resampling for diffusion models have been explored in recent preprints (e.g., Ma et al., Singhal et al.); while this paper distinguishes itself through gradient-based local Langevin search and robotics applications, the core algorithmic formulations of BFS particle filtering are quite closely related.

strengths: Unifying Conceptual Framework: The paper provides a clear conceptual bridge between classical search principles (local vs. global search) and diffusion model inference, categorizing gradient-based guidance with recurrence as local Langevin MCMC search and tree-based sampling as global exploration.

Theoretical Connection: Proposition 1 formalizes the relationship between recurrent training-free guidance and annealed Langevin MCMC in the continuous limit, offering a grounded explanation for why recurrence acts as a manifold-contracting force that mitigates out-of-distribution drift.

Multi-Domain Exploration: The empirical validation spans three distinct problem domains: long-horizon trajectory planning (PointMaze Giant and Ultra), offline reinforcement learning (D4RL locomotion), and image synthesis (CompBench and ImageNet).

Difficulty-Adaptive Compute Allocation: Demonstrating that DFS naturally backtracks more on difficult instances and less on simple instances (Figure 4c) provides a compelling demonstration of dynamic test-time compute allocation without requiring oracle problem difficulty labels.
weaknesses: Extremely Narrow ImageNet Evaluation: The conditional ImageNet experiment (Section 5.3.2) is evaluated on only two classes (labels 222 and 444) with 256 samples per class. Standard evaluation protocols in diffusion models require calculating FID over 50,000 samples across the full 1,000 classes; evaluating on two classes is statistically fragile and insufficient to draw broad conclusions.

Fragmented and Incomplete Algorithm Comparisons: The proposed global search variants (BFS-Resampling, BFS-Pruning, DFS) are not evaluated uniformly across tasks. In CompBench text-to-image generation, only DFS is compared against Best-of-N; in ImageNet, only BFS is evaluated; and in Offline RL, neither BFS nor DFS is used at all (reverting strictly to Best-of-N with 2–4 particles). A comprehensive head-to-head comparison between BFS and DFS across the same tasks is missing.

Heavy Hyperparameter Sensitivity: The framework introduces multiple sensitive hyperparameters per algorithm (evaluation schedule S, backtracking depth Delta_T, threshold schedule delta_t, temperature tau_t, guidance coefficients rho and mu, recurrence steps N_recur). As shown in Table 3, almost every sub-task in D4RL relies on a uniquely tuned hyperparameter configuration, raising questions regarding out-of-the-box generality without extensive tuning.

Incremental Algorithmic Novelty: The individual components—recurrent training-free guidance (e.g., FreeDoM, TFG), particle filtering/resampling at intermediate noise levels (e.g., SMC steering, Ma et al., 2025), and noise re-injection/backtracking (e.g., restart sampling, SDEdit)—are largely established in the literature. The primary contribution lies in framing them within classical search terminology.
